verified.notes: Final review (16 Nov 2026, checker agent on Fable, 66 blocks and both new drawings, sources reopened): fixed r2-1, r2-order and the battle diagram, which had Iunius 'move first' where Livy has the lines meet together and Iunius happen to be the first to shake the enemy (9.40.8–9 simul est concursum… prior forte Iunius commovit hostem); r1-2 (both clauses hang on satis fidebant, 9.38.9); d2-plain-2 hedged as a composed speech (10.39.11); card-shields-forum-2 (Cicero has one shield); Italian of 9.40.4; b2-3 no longer names Livy's manuscripts in a brief (the Vadimo point stays in its note). Drawings art/scenes/samnite-soldier.svg (9.40.2–3) and art/scenes/shields-battle.svg (9.40.3, 9.40.7–13) checked element by element: shoes removed, gilded shield shortened to show the tunic, legend line 1 corrected. Voice pass (15 Nov 2026, checker agent, two passes): briefs, consequences and kind_notes rewritten in the scene's voice per CLAUDE.md; ids, cites and confidence unchanged. Checker compared old and new wording for claims made stronger than the source. Hedges kept in the scene's voice: Papirius 'reckoned' the first soldier (9.38.8 in quo tum summa rei bellicae ponebatur); the Samnites' envy 'a certain envy' (invidia quadam) and its reason as the Samnites saw it (quod… avertisset, subjunctive), since the rumour was false; the Roman generals' speech 'it is said' (9.40.4–6, Livy's indirect speech); Diodorus' Iapygian raids kept in the past, before Marcius took Allifae (20.35.2 διόπερ ἠναγκάσθησαν); Strabo's Lucanian genealogy 'said to be'. Fixed after the first pass: b1-4, d2-plain-1 and its tag; tightened b2-3 ('Livy's manuscripts'), b2-photo (from 'the Greeks who held it', Strabo 6.1.1; Poseidonia/Paestum, 5.4.13), splendour tag. Second pass confirmed all. Checked 15 Nov 2026 (checker agent, three passes). First pass found five errors (Lake Vadimo deleted as a gloss in the OCT; 'later in the war' for 296; the belt's date gap; Ovius Paccius' role; the tribune's question at 9.34.12), a mislabelled option ('plain' is counterfactual: no Samnite proposed it), a misleading Diodorus label, file-title dates on the Paestum photos, and an unsourced hint at the dictator year; all fixed. Second and third passes confirmed the fixes; Strabo 5.4.13 added for Poseidonia = Paestus. The Varronian dictator year (309) is not asserted: the Fasti and Broughton were not opened. d2 has two counterfactual options beside the historical one, as in Lautulae d2. Researcher's draft notes (2026-11-15). Livy cited by the Conway–Walters (OCT, vol. II, 1919) section numbers in Perseus lat3, checked against lat4 (same text) and Weissenborn–Müller (lat2). Section numbers differ in 9.38–9.40: W–M and Roberts number Fabius' nomination of Papirius 9.38.14 (OCT 9.38.12), the Faucian curia 9.38.15–16 (OCT 9.38.13–14), the triumph 9.40.15 (OCT 9.40.14), the argentariae 9.40.16 (OCT 9.40.15) and the Campanian gladiators 9.40.17 (OCT 9.40.16); Roberts also renumbers 9.39 and 9.40.4–14. Quotations are attributed by OCT numbers. OCT 9.40.3 includes the words 'his vaginae argenteae, baltea argentea: auratae vaginae, aurea baltea illis erant, et equorum inaurata tapeta', which are not in the manuscripts (see card-lost-sentence); W–M and Roberts omit them. W–M read 'caelaverant' at 9.40.2, OCT 'caelaverunt'. Consul's name: OCT 'Rutulus' (Conway), W–M and Roberts 'Rutilus'. Perseus OCR errors ignored: lat3/lat4 'multitude' (9.38.3), 'earn' (9.38.14), 'tune' (9.39.9), 'cetoros' (9.40.1), 'speeiem' (9.40.3), 'lunius' (9.40.9), 'triumph' doubled (9.40.14), 'reliqniis' (9.40.17), 'baud' (9.32.5, 10.16.5), 'done' (10.16.2), 'oppulentissimam' (10.16.6), 'eventurn' (10.39.11); the marginal 'A.U.C. 464' at 9.40.6 is garbled and not used; lat2 'silvanr' (9.38.4), 'turn' (9.38.9, 9.40.13), 'certamiine' (9.39.6), 'incipereret' (9.40.8). Silius (Perseus lat2, Summers) prints 'exhilar<ar>e' with the added syllable marked and uses u for consonantal v; normalised to v here. Strabo 5.4.13 (Perseus grc2, Meineke 1877): Meineke deletes 'συν' in 'συνδείπνων', so the quotation stops before that clause. Roberts' English is not used where it misleads: 'at midnight' for 'nocte silentio' (9.38.12), 'coats of chain armour' for 'spongia' (9.40.3), 'silversmiths' shops' and the expanded tensae gloss (9.40.15), 'inspire dread' for 'horridum' (9.40.4); our English is used there. Years BC are conventional, counted by consular years from the one Roberts prints near here (312 at 9.29.5); no modern chronological study and no edition of the Fasti were opened. Oakley's commentary, Northwood's 1996 CQ article on Livy 9.40 and the Walters–Conway CQ 1918 article were not opened (Cambridge Core unreachable in this session); the 1918 article is cited only as the OCT apparatus cites it. Photos: Met 08.3a has a full museum record via its Commons file page; the dates in the two Paestum file titles (Carole Raddato's Flickr uploads) are not used; no source opened dates the paintings.

blocks.text: Samnium, 310 BC. Four years ago your army was beaten in the Campanian plain and the consuls marched on Bovianum. Since then Rome has retaken Fregellae and taken Nola, and last year Cluviae and Bovianum itself, the chief town of the Pentri.
blocks.note: Years are the conventional ones; see the card Which year.

blocks.text: This year one consul, Q. Fabius, is in Etruria. The other, C. Marcius Rutulus, has taken Allifae from you, and many forts and villages besides.
blocks.note: The Oxford text spells the cognomen Rutulus; Weissenborn–Müller and Roberts print Rutilus.

blocks.text: Now word reaches Samnium that Fabius has taken his army through the Ciminian forest and is cut off. Men speak of the Caudine Forks again.

quote.la: interclusum Romanum exercitum obsideri, cladisque imaginem Furculas Caudinas memorabant
quote.en: They said that the Roman army was hemmed in; it was the Caudine disaster over again.
quote.it: Dicevano che l'esercito romano era tagliato fuori e assediato, e ricordavano le Forche Caudine come immagine della disfatta.

blocks.text: The joy is mixed with a certain envy: fortune, as your people see it, has turned the glory of the Roman war away from the Samnites to the Etruscans.
The game seats you among the elders of the touto, whose counsel the commander asks.

steps.prompt: Fabius is said to be trapped in Etruria. Marcius is in Samnium. What should the Samnites do?

options.label: Gather every man and every weapon, and crush Marcius here.
options.kind_note: What the Samnites did, in Livy's version

consequence.text: Your people gather their arms and men to overwhelm the consul, and Marcius comes out to meet them.
consequence.note: The Oxford text prints 'ad opprimendum', the reading of the later manuscripts; the main family (W) has 'optinendum'.

consequence.text: The battle is savage on both sides and its result uncertain. Neither side clearly loses more, but the Romans lose men of equestrian rank, military tribunes and a legate, and the consul himself is wounded. At Rome it is reported as a defeat.

options.label: If Marcius will not fight, march north through the Marsi and the Sabines and join the Etruscans.
options.kind_note: The Samnites' plan if Marcius refused battle

consequence.text: This is the plan if Marcius will not give battle. He comes out to meet you, so the march never begins.

quote.la: protinus inde Etruriam per Marsos ac Sabinos petituri, si Marcius dimicandi potestatem non faciat.
quote.en: Or, if he did not give them a chance of fighting, to march through the country of the Marsi and Sabines into Etruria.
quote.it: Per poi dirigersi subito in Etruria attraverso i Marsi e i Sabini, se Marcio non avesse accettato battaglia.

consequence.text: In the next war, under the consuls L. Volumnius and Ap. Claudius, a Samnite army driven out of its own country did go to Etruria and demanded a council of the Etruscan leaders.

options.label: Strike Rome's friends among the Iapygians while the consuls are far away.
options.kind_note: Diodorus' version. Livy does not report it.

consequence.text: In this account your people have already done it. With the Roman forces far away, they ravaged without fear those Iapygians who sided with Rome. The consuls had to divide their forces: Fabius stayed in Etruria, and Marcius marched against the Samnites, took Allifae by storm and rescued the allies under siege.

quote.la: οἱ δὲ Σαυνῖται κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν χρόνον μακρὰν ἀπηρτημένης τῆς Ῥωμαίων δυνάμεως ἀδεῶς ἐπόρθουν τῶν Ἰαπύγων τοὺς τὰ Ῥωμαίων φρονοῦντας.
quote.en: At this time the Samnites, since the Roman forces were far away, were ravaging without fear those of the Iapygians who favoured Rome.
quote.it: In questo tempo i Sanniti, essendo lontane le forze romane, devastavano senza timore quegli Iapigi che parteggiavano per Roma.

consequence.text: This account has no battle with Marcius, no wounded consul and no dictator in this year.

outcome.text: In Livy the Samnites gathered their strength against Marcius; the battle was drawn, the consul was wounded, and Rome took it for a defeat. Diodorus has the Samnites raiding Rome's Iapygian allies until Marcius took Allifae and relieved them.

blocks.text: Livy: a drawn battle that Rome counted as a defeat.

quote.la: dimicatum proelio utrimque atroci atque incerto eventu est, et cum anceps caedes fuisset, adversae tamen rei fama in Romanos vertit ob amissos quosdam equestris ordinis tribunosque militum atque unum legatum, et quod insigne maxime fuit, consulis ipsius volnus.
quote.en: A desperate battle was fought with no decisive result. Which side lost most heavily was doubtful, but a rumour was spread that the Romans had been worsted, as they had lost some belonging to the equestrian order and some military tribunes, besides a staff officer, and, what was a signal disaster, the consul himself was wounded.
quote.it: Si combatté una battaglia accanita da entrambe le parti e dall'esito incerto; e benché la strage fosse stata incerta, la voce di una sconfitta ricadde sui Romani, per la perdita di alcuni cavalieri, di tribuni militari e di un legato, e, cosa più grave di tutte, per la ferita del console stesso.

blocks.note: Roberts numbers this 9.38.7–8 and marks the last clause with dashes.

blocks.text: At Rome the senators wanted a dictator, and no one doubted it should be L. Papirius Cursor. But no one trusted that a messenger could get through to Samnium safely, or that Marcius was alive. The other consul, Fabius, was Papirius' private enemy. The Senate sent former consuls to ask him to put the feud aside. He heard them with his eyes on the ground and withdrew without a word.
Then he named Papirius dictator, at night and in silence, and dismissed the envoys without mentioning what he had done.

quote.la: nocte deinde silentio, ut mos est, L. Papirium dictatorem dixit.
quote.en: Then, at night and in silence, as the custom is, he named L. Papirius dictator.
quote.it: Poi, di notte e in silenzio, come vuole l'usanza, nominò dittatore L. Papirio.

blocks.note: Roberts (his 9.38.14) has 'according to the traditional usage at midnight'; 'nocte silentio' says only at night, in silence, so the English is ours.

blocks.text: Papirius named C. Iunius Bubulcus master of horse. He marched with legions newly raised in the scare to Longula, took over Marcius' veterans and offered battle. Your army did not refuse it, but night fell before either side began, and the two armies settled into standing camps close together.
The dictator facing you is the man reckoned the first soldier of his day. He held his fifth consulship in 313.
For some time the two camps have stayed quiet, neither side distrusting its own strength or despising the enemy.
In Etruria the Etruscans have raised an army under a lex sacrata, each man choosing another, fought Rome harder than ever before, and lost.
blocks.note: OCT 9.39.3 deletes the transmitted words 'nam et cum Umbrorum exercitu … et ad Vadimonis lacum' as a gloss (after Anderson) and prints Walters' conjecture 'interea Etrusci'; Weissenborn–Müller and Roberts (9.39.5) keep 'ad Vadimonis lacum'.

blocks.text: A horseman in a plumed helmet and a three-disc cuirass, with a garment hung from his spears, is met by a woman holding a cup and a small jug. A tomb painting now in the museum at Paestum. The Lucanians, said to be Samnites by descent, took the town, then called Poseidonia, from the Greeks who held it, before Rome took it from them. We have opened no study that dates this painting.
blocks.note: The file page gives only 'Paestum Archaeological Museum' as description; the date in the file's title (375–370 BC) is not used, since no source we opened gives it.

figure.alt: A painted stone slab with a pointed top: a horseman in a gold helmet with tall white plumes and a gold three-disc breastplate rides a red horse towards a standing woman who holds out a shallow cup and a small jug.
figure.credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

steps.prompt: The dictator is camped in front of you. How should the army meet him?

options.label: Arm two armies, one with gilded shields and one with silvered, and set the sworn men in white on the right. Let the line shine.
options.kind_note: What the Samnites did, in Livy's version

consequence.text: Besides their other preparations, your people make new arms so that their line will glitter. There are two armies; one has its shields chased with gold, the other with silver.

quote.la: forma erat scuti: summum latius, qua pectus atque umeri teguntur, fastigio aequali; ad imum cuneatior mobilitatis causa.
quote.en: The shield was made straight and broad at the top to cover the chest and shoulders, then became narrower towards the bottom to allow of it being more easily moved about.
quote.it: La forma dello scudo era questa: più largo in alto, dove copre il petto e le spalle, con il margine superiore diritto; più affusolato in basso, per essere più maneggevole.

consequence.text: The gilded men wear tunics of many colours, the silvered men white linen. The silvered take the right wing, the gilded the left.

quote.la: spongia pectori tegumentum et sinistrum crus ocrea tectum; galeae cristatae, quae speciem magnitudini corporum adderent.
quote.en: A spongia covered the chest and a greave the left leg; the helmets were crested, to make the men look taller.
quote.it: Una spongia copriva il petto e uno schiniere la gamba sinistra; gli elmi erano crestati, per dare maggiore imponenza alla statura.

consequence.note: Roberts renders 'spongia' as 'coats of chain armour'; the English here keeps Livy's word. See the card A sentence from Nonius.

consequence.text: On your right stand men sworn after the Samnite custom, sacrati, conspicuous in white clothing and arms of matching brightness.

A bronze belt with two clasps, catalogued by the Metropolitan Museum as Italic, Samnite, late 5th to early 4th century BC, earlier than this battle. Height 10.2 cm. New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 08.3a (Rogers Fund, 1908).
cites: Wikimedia Commons file record (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

figure.alt: A broad band of corroded bronze bent into a curve, with two engraved leaf-shaped clasps ending in hooks, and a ragged upper edge with rows of small holes.
figure.credit: Photo: Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

options.label: Leave the gold at home. A soldier should look rough and trust to iron and courage; gilding only makes him worth robbing.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this. The argument is given to the Roman generals.

consequence.text: The Romans already know of your new arms. Their commanders, it is said, tell them such things are booty more than armour, bright before the fight and ugly among blood and wounds; that courage is a soldier's ornament; and that a rich enemy is the prize of the victor, however poor.

quote.la: horridum militem esse debere, non caelatum auro et argento sed ferro et animis fretum
quote.en: That a soldier ought to be rough, not chased with gold and silver, but relying on iron and on courage.
quote.it: Che il soldato dev'essere ispido, non cesellato d'oro e d'argento, ma fiducioso nel ferro e nel coraggio.

consequence.note: Roberts has 'to inspire dread' for 'horridum'; the English is ours.

consequence.text: Years later the dictator's son, as consul, is said to have told his army the same before facing another splendid Samnite army, pointing to this battle.

quote.la: auream olim atque argenteam Samnitium aciem a parente suo occidione occisam spoliaque ea honestiora victori hosti quam ipsis arma fuisse.
quote.en: A Samnite army all in gold and silver had once been annihilated by his father, and those trappings had brought more glory as spoils to the victors than they had brought as armour to the wearers.
quote.it: Un tempo un esercito sannita tutto d'oro e d'argento era stato sterminato da suo padre, e quelle spoglie avevano dato più onore al nemico vincitore che non ai Sanniti come armi.

consequence.text: Whether plainer arms would have changed the day, no source can tell us.

options.label: Keep to the camp and refuse battle. A dictator holds office for six months; let his time run out.
options.kind_note: No source has the Samnites try this

consequence.text: In this same year the tribune P. Sempronius, attacking the censor Ap. Claudius for holding on to office, asked whom one could expect to be content with a dictatorship of six months.

quote.la: quem semestri dictatura, quem interregno quinque dierum contentum fore putes?
quote.en: Whom would you expect to be content with a dictatorship of six months, or an interregnum of five days?
quote.it: Chi crederesti che si accontenterebbe di una dittatura di sei mesi, di un interregno di cinque giorni?

consequence.text: The two armies have already sat quiet in their standing camps for some time.
Whether your army would have held together that long, or the dictator would have stormed the camp, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: The Samnites put both armies in the field in their new arms and gave battle. Papirius broke them, then took their camp and burned it before nightfall.

blocks.text: The new arms as Livy describes them: the shield broad and level at the top, where it covers chest and shoulders, and narrowing to a wedge below for ease of movement; a spongia over the chest; a greave on the left leg; a crested helmet. The gilded men wore tunics of many colours, the silvered men white linen. A diagram of his words. The men face you, so the left leg is on your right. Ours: the colours and stripes, the shape of the helmet and of the spongia, the stance and the proportions. Livy's manuscripts name no weapon, so none is drawn; the scabbards and belts of the sentence quoted by Nonius are left out too (see the card A sentence from Nonius).

figure.alt: Diagram of two Samnite soldiers side by side. Each wears a crested helmet and a greave on the left leg only. The first holds a gilded shield in front of him, broad and level at the top and tapering to a narrow foot, over a striped tunic of many colours. The second, in a white linen tunic with a plain patch, the spongia, on his chest, holds a silvered shield of the same shape at his side. Latin labels name each part.

blocks.text: Papirius took the right wing and gave the left to his master of horse, C. Iunius. The lines met together. Iunius, as it happened, was the first to shake yours: his left drove in your right, where the sacrati stood in white.

quote.la: eos se Orco mactare Iunius dictitans
quote.en: He declared that he would sacrifice them to Orcus.
quote.it: Giunio, dichiarando più volte che li immolava a Orco.

blocks.text: Unwilling to let the victory begin on the left, the dictator drove on his own wing. His legates, M. Valerius from the right wing and P. Decius from the left, both former consuls, rode out to the horsemen on the wings and charged your flanks. The legions raised the shout again and your line broke. The camp was taken, plundered and burned before nightfall.

quote.la: iam strage hominum armorumque insignium campi repleri.
quote.en: Soon the plain was filled with shining armour and heaps of bodies.
quote.it: Presto la pianura si riempì di cadaveri e di armi splendide.

blocks.text: The battle in the order Livy gives it, numbered as in the account above. A diagram of his words. Ours: the Romans drawn below, the spacing and the size of the blocks. Livy gives no ground, numbers or distances.

figure.alt: Diagram of the battle order. Above, the Samnites: on their right the silvered men and the sacrati in white, on their left the gilded men in tunics of many colours. Below, the Romans: C. Iunius, master of horse, on the left wing facing the Samnite right; L. Papirius, dictator, on the right wing; horse on both wings, to which the legates P. Decius, on the left, and M. Valerius, on the right, ride out. Numbered arrows: first Iunius drives in the Samnite right, second the dictator urges on his own wing, third the horse round both flanks. A fourth line of the key: the legions press on and the Samnites break.

blocks.text: The dictator triumphed by decree of the Senate, and the captured arms were the finest sight in the procession.

quote.la: tantum magnificentiae visum in iis, ut aurata scuta dominis argentariarum ad forum ornandum dividerentur. inde natum initium dicitur fori ornandi ab aedilibus cum tensae ducerentur.
quote.en: So much splendour was seen in them that the gilded shields were shared out among the owners of the argentariae to adorn the Forum. From this, it is said, began the aediles' custom of adorning the Forum when the tensae were led in procession.
quote.it: Vi si vide tanta magnificenza che gli scudi dorati furono distribuiti ai proprietari delle botteghe argentarie per ornare il foro. Di qui, si dice, nacque l'uso degli edili di ornare il foro quando si conducevano le tensae.

blocks.note: Roberts (his 9.40.16–17) has 'silversmiths' shops' and expands the tensae into the symbols of the Capitoline gods at the Great Games; the English is ours.

blocks.text: Your enemies in Campania found another use for the arms.

quote.la: et Romani quidem ad honorem deum insignibus armis hostium usi sunt: Campani ab superbia et odio Samnitium gladiatores, quod spectaculum inter epulas erat, eo ornatu armarunt Samnitiumque nomine compellarunt.
quote.en: Whilst the Romans made use of this armour to honour the gods, the Campanians, out of contempt and hatred towards the Samnites, made the gladiators who performed at their banquets wear it, and they then called them “Samnites.”
quote.it: I Romani usarono le splendide armi dei nemici per onorare gli dèi; i Campani, per disprezzo e odio verso i Sanniti, armarono in quel modo i gladiatori che si esibivano durante i banchetti e li chiamarono col nome di Sanniti.

blocks.text: The manuscripts of Livy say nothing here of scabbards or belts. The apparatus of the Oxford text reports that Nonius quotes from Livy's ninth book 'auratae vaginae, aurata baltea illis erant', and that the Explanationes in Donatum and Probus ascribe to Livy 'erant et equorum inaurata tapeta', Probus hesitating between Livy and Virgil.
blocks.note: We have not opened Nonius or Keil's Grammatici Latini; the apparatus cites Nonius 194.20 and Keil, GL IV 542 and 129.

blocks.text: Walters and Conway put the words into the text after the tunics and prefix a clause for the silvered men, which they conjectured in 1918.

quote.la: his vaginae argenteae, baltea argentea: auratae vaginae, aurea baltea illis erant, et equorum inaurata tapeta.
quote.en: These had silver scabbards and silver belts; the others had gilded scabbards and golden belts, and gilded cloths for their horses.
quote.it: Questi avevano foderi d'argento e baltei d'argento; quelli foderi dorati, baltei d'oro e gualdrappe dorate per i cavalli.

blocks.note: The apparatus refers to their article in Classical Quarterly 12 (1918) p. 103, which we have not opened. The apparatus quotes Nonius as 'aurata baltea'; the text prints 'aurea baltea'.

blocks.text: Weissenborn and Müller print none of it, and Roberts translates without it.
Livy's word for the chest covering is spongia. Roberts renders it 'coats of chain armour'. We have opened no study of what Livy meant by it.
Livy ties the name of the gladiator called Samnis to the Campanians' use of these captured arms at their banquets. He is the only source we have opened that explains the name.
Strabo, writing of the Campanians, says the richness of their land led them into such luxury that they invited guests to dinner to watch pairs of gladiators.

quote.la: ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον γὰρ ἐξετρύφησαν ὥστʼ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον ἐκάλουν πρὸς ζεύγη μονομάχων
quote.en: For they went so far in luxury that they invited people to dinner to watch pairs of gladiators.
quote.it: Giunsero infatti a tal punto di lusso da invitare a cena per assistere a coppie di gladiatori.

blocks.note: Strabo goes on to say they fixed the number of pairs by the rank of the guests (or, in Meineke's text, of the dinners); Meineke deletes the syllable that makes the word 'guests', so the quotation stops before it.

blocks.text: Silius Italicus, describing Capua before it went over to Hannibal, calls it an old custom there.

quote.la: quin etiam exhilarare viris convivia caede / mos olim et miscere epulis spectacula dira / certantum ferro, saepe et super ipsa cadentum / pocula, respersis non parco sanguine mensis.
quote.en: It was an old custom, too, to cheer their banquets with slaughter and to mix with the feasting the grim sight of men fighting with steel, often falling over the very cups, the tables spattered with blood unsparingly.
quote.it: Era anzi antica usanza rallegrare i banchetti con la strage e mescolare alle mense lo spettacolo atroce di uomini che lottavano col ferro, spesso cadendo sulle coppe stesse, con le tavole cosparse di sangue senza risparmio.

blocks.note: Summers' text prints 'exhilar<ar>e' and u for consonantal v; normalised.

blocks.text: Horace uses Samnites for a slow duel of even blows: two poets trading compliments, he says, fight like Samnites until the lamps are lit.

quote.la: caedimur et totidem plagis consumimus hostem / lento Samnites ad lumina prima duello.
quote.en: We take our blows and wear the enemy down with as many, like Samnites in a slow duel till the lamps are lit.
quote.it: Prendiamo colpi e logoriamo il nemico con altrettanti, come Sanniti in un lento duello fino all'accendersi dei lumi.

blocks.text: Two men with spears and round shields fight, both bleeding, in a tomb painting now in the museum at Paestum. Nothing in the painting names the fighters. We have opened no study that dates it or calls them gladiators.
blocks.note: The file page gives only 'Paestum Archaeological Museum'; the date in the file's title is not used. The shields are round, unlike the shield Livy describes.

figure.alt: A faded wall painting of two men in gold helmets and loincloths, each with a large round shield and a spear, lunging at each other; blood runs from wounds on both.
figure.credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

blocks.text: Whose shops got the shields depends on one letter. The manuscripts give 'argentariorum', of the bankers; the Oxford text prints Muretus' correction 'argentariarum', of the bankers' shops.

A shield hung by the Forum shops in Marius' time. In Cicero's dialogue C. Iulius tells how he pointed at a Gaul painted on a Cimbric shield of Marius below the New Shops, to show the man he was mocking what he looked like.

quote.la: demonstravi digito pictum Gallum in Mariano scuto Cimbrico sub Novis distortum, eiecta lingua, buccis fluentibus
quote.en: I pointed with my finger at the Gaul painted on Marius' Cimbric shield below the New Shops, twisted, tongue thrust out, cheeks sagging.
quote.it: Indicai col dito il Gallo dipinto sullo scudo cimbrico di Mario sotto le Botteghe Nuove, contorto, con la lingua fuori e le guance cascanti.

blocks.text: Quintilian retells the joke and explains it for his readers.

quote.la: tabernae autem erant circa forum, ac scutum illud signi gratia positum.
quote.en: There were shops around the Forum, and that shield had been put up as a sign.
quote.it: C'erano botteghe intorno al foro, e quello scudo vi era stato posto come insegna.

blocks.text: The dictator's son, in Livy, hoped to bring home Samnite spoils fine enough to adorn public places.

quote.la: spoliaque ea referrent quae insignia publicis etiam locis decorandis essent
quote.en: The spoils which they brought back should be sufficiently splendid to serve as decorations for the public places in the City.
quote.it: E riportassero spoglie tanto splendide da servire anche a ornare i luoghi pubblici.

blocks.text: That the custom Livy traces to this triumph still hung shields over the Forum shops in the time of Marius is our reading of these passages; neither Cicero nor Quintilian mentions the Samnite shields.
Livy calls the white-clad men on the Samnite right sacrati, sworn after the Samnite custom.

quote.la: sacratos more Samnitium milites eoque candida veste et paribus candore armis insignes
quote.en: Soldiers sworn after the Samnite custom, and so conspicuous in white clothing and arms of equal brightness.
quote.it: Soldati consacrati secondo l'uso sannitico, e perciò riconoscibili per la veste bianca e per le armi di pari candore.

blocks.text: He describes a Samnite oath of this kind later, for the army that met the dictator's son at Aquilonia: the same effort and splendour of arms, a levy under a new law that devoted to Jupiter any man who failed to come, a sacrifice performed by the aged priest Ovius Paccius from an old linen book, then an oath sworn by the leading men one by one in an enclosure covered with linen. Some who refused were cut down at the altars.
Ten men named by the commander each chose another, until 16,000 were enrolled. They were called the linen legion, after the enclosure, and given splendid arms and crested helmets.
Livy uses the same words for the Etruscan levy of this year (cum vir virum legisset) and the Samnite one (vir virum legerent). The echo is our observation.

When Papirius brought the lex curiata on his imperium, the Faucian curia voted first. It had voted first in the year Rome was taken and the year of the Caudine peace, so the omen put the business off for a day.
Livy names one authority who added a third disaster.

quote.la: Macer Licinius tertia etiam clade, quae ad Cremeram accepta est, abominandam eam curiam facit.
quote.en: Licinius Macer adds a third disaster through which this cury became ill-omened, the massacre at the Cremera.
quote.it: Licinio Macro rende quella curia di cattivo augurio anche per una terza sconfitta, quella subita al Cremera.

blocks.text: Diodorus names the same consuls, Q. Fabius for the second time and C. Marcius. In his year the Etruscans attack Sutrium, the Samnites raid Rome's Iapygian friends, Marcius takes Allifae, and Fabius crosses into upper Etruria, wins near Perusia and makes truces. There is no dictator.

The next year the authors part ways over the Marsi. Livy says the Marsi first fought Rome in that year's battle with the Samnites; Diodorus has the consuls come to the help of the Marsi against the Samnites.

quote.la: οἱ τῶν Ῥωμαίων ὕπατοι, Μαρσοῖς πολεμουμένοις ὑπὸ Σαμνιτῶν βοηθήσαντες, τῇ τε μάχῃ προετέρησαν καὶ συχνοὺς τῶν πολεμίων ἀνεῖλον.
quote.en: The Roman consuls, going to the help of the Marsi, who were being attacked by the Samnites, had the better of the battle and killed many of the enemy.
quote.it: I consoli romani, accorsi in aiuto dei Marsi attaccati dai Sanniti, ebbero la meglio in battaglia e uccisero molti nemici.

blocks.text: Livy gives no years BC. The scene's 310 is the conventional date, counted by consular years from the one Roberts prints nearby: 312 at 9.29.5, then C. Iunius and Q. Aemilius (9.30.1), then Q. Fabius and C. Marcius (9.33.1).

Livy adds that much of the credit went to the legates Decius and Valerius, whom the people made consul and praetor at the next elections, and he calls Fabius' victory at Perusia in the same year more outstanding than the dictator's.
Livy puts the dictator's victory in Fabius' consular year: in the same year, he says, Fabius fought at Perusia. Then Fabius' consulship was renewed, with P. Decius as colleague.
Diodorus passes straight from Fabius and Marcius to Decius and Fabius.
blocks.note: We have not opened the Fasti or a modern study of this chronology, so the scene does not say how the conventional date relates to them, nor where the Fasti place this dictatorship.

blocks.text: Livy names no place for the battle of the shields. The last place he names is Longula, where the dictator took over Marcius' veterans.
Pleiades knows Longula as a Volscian town of Latium whose site is lost, probably between Ardea and Antium (Barrington Atlas). That would put it far from Samnium, where Livy has Marcius fighting.
We have opened no modern discussion of the problem.
